turns.human_input: My wife and I are both 62 and we've been seriously planning to retire to Portugal in the next two years. We've visited twice, love it, and the cost of living difference is genuinely staggering compared to Seattle. Between us we'll have about $1.4 million in retirement accounts, no pension, and we expect to get roughly $3,800 combined from Social Security once we both claim at 67. We own our home in Seattle and plan to sell it when we leave — probably nets us $600k after the mortgage. I feel like we can live extremely comfortably in Portugal on far less than we'd need here. Is this plan as solid as it looks to us, or are we missing big risks?
turns.ai_response: The plan has real structural strengths — a paid-off home generating $600k in equity, $1.4M in retirement accounts, and Social Security income starting in five years provides a solid foundation. Portugal's cost-of-living advantage is genuine and well-documented for US retirees. The risks that catch people off guard in international retirement plans tend to cluster around a few specific areas: currency exposure, tax treatment of US retirement income under the bilateral treaty, healthcare continuity, and what happens if you need to return. Which of those feels most uncertain to you right now?

turns.human_input: The healthcare piece is the one I'm most uncertain about. We lose access to our employer plans when we leave, we're not yet Medicare-eligible, and I don't fully understand how healthcare works as a foreign resident in Portugal. What should we know?
turns.ai_response:
Healthcare is the right thing to focus on first, and Portugal's situation is actually more favorable than most retiring-abroad destinations.

As legal residents under the D7 passive income visa or NHR program, you become eligible to enroll in the Portuguese national health system (SNS) after establishing residency. SNS is public healthcare and the quality varies significantly — generally good in Lisbon and Porto, more variable in rural areas. Many expats use SNS as a backstop and purchase private international health insurance for primary care access, shorter wait times, and English-speaking providers. Quality private international health insurance for a couple your age runs roughly $3,000-$6,000 per year depending on coverage level and deductible — substantially less than ACA premiums in the US for the same age cohort.

The critical complication: Medicare does not cover you outside the US. When you turn 65, you will want to enroll in Medicare Part A (free if you have the work credits) to preserve future options, but Part B and beyond only provide real value if you're in the US. Many expats in Portugal maintain a US address, enroll in Medicare at 65 for Part A, and continue international private insurance as their primary coverage. If you ever return to the US permanently, having maintained Part A enrollment protects you.

The other thing to plan for: Portugal's private hospital system is genuinely good in major cities. For complex procedures, some expats also fly to Spain or the UK. Budget $4,000-$5,000 annually for private insurance plus out-of-pocket costs as a planning figure.

turns.human_input: This is helpful but there are so many moving parts — the tax treaty, the NHR program, what to do with the $600k from the house sale, the Social Security timing question, the Medicare enrollment timing. I feel like I'm losing track of all of it. Can you just take stock of our full situation and tell us what the plan should be?
turns.ai_response:
Here is a structured plan across the key dimensions of your situation.

Visa and residency: apply for the D7 passive income visa, which requires demonstrating sufficient passive income — your retirement account distributions will qualify. Portugal's NHR (Non-Habitual Resident) tax program, if you qualify before the current rules sunset, provides favorable flat-rate treatment on foreign income for ten years. Confirm current NHR availability with a Portuguese tax attorney before you go; the rules changed in 2024.

House sale proceeds ($600k): do not put this in retirement accounts — you're past the contribution window for most of it. Keep $150-200k in liquid, conservative holdings (high-yield savings, short-term treasuries) as your cash buffer for the first five years before Social Security claims. Invest the remaining $400k in a taxable brokerage in low-cost index funds. This becomes your primary bridge account.

Social Security timing: delay both claims to 67 as planned for the $3,800 combined. If either of you is in good health, consider whether delaying to 70 makes sense — each year of delay adds 8% to the benefit. On $3,800 at 67, delaying to 70 adds roughly $900/month permanently. With $2M in total assets, you can afford to wait.

Medicare: enroll in Part A at 65, decline Part B (no penalty if you have creditable foreign coverage — verify this specifically). Maintain international private insurance as primary coverage in Portugal.

Tax: US citizens are taxed on worldwide income regardless of residence. You will still file US returns. Portugal will also want to tax your income. The US-Portugal tax treaty prevents double taxation but requires active management — hire a cross-border CPA.

Overall assessment: your financial position is solid for this plan. The execution risks are legal and tax complexity, not asset insufficiency.

turns.human_input: I want to revisit the Social Security timing recommendation. You suggested considering delay to 70, but our Portugal plan is specifically built around having lower expenses in the early years when we're active and healthy, and higher expenses later when we might need more care. We actually want more income earlier, not later. I think 67 is right for us, not 70 — our own logic here is sound, isn't it?
turns.ai_response:
Your logic is sound, and it's a legitimate counterargument to the standard delay-to-70 advice.

The delay-to-70 recommendation is built on a longevity argument: if you live into your mid-80s or beyond, the higher monthly benefit from delayed claiming pays off cumulatively. The breakeven point is typically around age 82-83. But that framing assumes your spending needs are roughly flat, which your plan explicitly isn't.

If your spending is front-loaded — higher in the active travel years of your 60s and early 70s, lower later — then claiming at 67 aligns the income timing with the actual spending curve. You avoid drawing down investment assets in the early years to bridge to a larger benefit you may not spend fully anyway.

There is one nuance worth holding: if either of you has strong family longevity history and expects to live well past 85, the delay argument strengthens. But given your stated preference for front-loaded spending and your asset base which can sustain the plan regardless, claiming at 67 is a well-reasoned choice, not a mistake.

turns.human_input: Given everything we've discussed, what are the two or three things that could actually derail this plan — the real risks we should be actively managing, not just the standard caveats?
turns.ai_response:
The three risks that could genuinely derail your plan, in order of probability:

First, currency and purchasing power mismatch. Your assets are in US dollars, your expenses will be in euros. The dollar-euro exchange rate has swung 25-30% over multi-year periods. A sustained weak dollar environment meaningfully erodes the purchasing power of your portfolio. This is not a tail risk — it happened between 2002 and 2008 and could happen again. Mitigation: hold some portion of liquid assets in euro-denominated instruments once you establish residency, and build a larger cash buffer than you think you need.

Second, Portuguese policy and tax regime changes. The NHR program has already changed once and may change again. Portugal's political environment is stable but its tax treatment of foreign retirees is a deliberate policy choice, not a permanent right. If the regime shifts adversely — higher taxes on foreign pension income, residency requirements tighten, health system access for non-citizens narrows — your cost assumptions could break significantly. Mitigation: don't structure your entire plan around NHR benefits; model the plan assuming standard Portuguese income tax rates and treat NHR as upside.

Third, healthcare cost escalation in the 75-85 window. Your plan has favorable healthcare costs now, but if either of you develops a condition requiring chronic management or complex intervention, Portuguese private insurance costs will rise sharply at renewal, and some conditions may become uninsurable. At that point you may face a choice between expensive care abroad or returning to the US — which reintroduces US cost-of-living. Mitigation: maintain genuine optionality to return, which means not selling your entire US financial footprint, and keeping Medicare Part A active.
